topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: Which two commands manage password aging attributes on a local account? (Select all that apply.)
options: chage
passwd
usermod
useradd
explanation: chage and passwd both write the aging fields (3–8) of /etc/shadow. usermod can set account and password expiry too, but its role in this chapter is locking and unlocking.

topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: Using chage, set mindays to 7, maxdays to 90 and warndays to 10 for the account user100.
explanation: Note the case: lowercase -m is the minimum days, uppercase -M the maximum, and -W the warning period. The passwd equivalents are -n, -x and -w respectively.

topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: What does `chage -d 0 user60` do?
options: Forces user60 to change their password at next login
Disables password aging for user60
Expires the account immediately so user60 cannot log in
Removes user60's password
explanation: Field 3 is the last-change date in days since the UNIX epoch; setting it to 0 makes the password look infinitely old, so a change is demanded at next login. `passwd -e user60` achieves the same thing.

topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: Display the current password aging settings for the account user5.
explanation: chage -l prints the last change date, password and account expiry, inactivity period and the min/max/warning values. passwd -S user5 gives a terser one-line status.

topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: How do you disable the account expiry date that was previously set with chage -E?
options: chage -E -1 <user>
chage -E 0 <user>
chage -E never <user>
chage -d -1 <user>
explanation: -1 turns the feature off. The same convention applies to -I -1 (inactivity) and -M -1 (maximum age).

topic: Enforce Password Security Policies with Aging Attributes
prompt: Which file holds the system-wide default password aging settings applied to new accounts?
options: /etc/login.defs
/etc/shadow
/etc/default/useradd
/etc/security/pwquality.conf
explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS and PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs are the defaults. Per-user values live in fields 3–8 of /etc/shadow.

topic: Lock and Unlock User Accounts to Control System Access
prompt: What does locking an account with `usermod -L` actually change?
options: It prepends an exclamation mark to the password hash in /etc/shadow
It sets the shell to /sbin/nologin
It deletes the password hash entirely
It sets the account expiry date to today
explanation: The leading ! makes the stored hash unmatchable, so no password can authenticate. usermod -U or passwd -u removes it; passwd -l is the equivalent lock.

topic: Lock and Unlock User Accounts to Control System Access
prompt: Which commands can lock a user account? (Select all that apply.)
options: usermod -L
passwd -l
chage -l
passwd -d
explanation: usermod -L and passwd -l both lock. chage -l merely lists aging settings, and passwd -d deletes the password without expiring the account — which leaves it passwordless, not locked.

prompt: Create a group named linuxadm with GID 5000.
explanation: -g assigns a specific GID; without it the next free GID from the login.defs range is used. -r creates a system group with a GID between 1 and 999.

prompt: Add user1 to the supplementary group dba without disturbing their existing group memberships.
explanation: -G alone REPLACES the supplementary group list; -a appends to it. Forgetting -a is a classic way to silently drop a user out of every other group.

prompt: Rename the group linuxadm to sysadm.
explanation: -n takes the new name first, then the existing group name. Renaming replaces the original entry — the old group name no longer exists.

prompt: What does the -o option do for groupadd and groupmod?
options: Permits a GID that duplicates an existing group's, so the system treats them as one
Overwrites the group if it already exists
Makes the group the owner of new files
Marks the group as a system group
explanation: -o (--non-unique) waives the uniqueness check on the GID. useradd has the same option for UIDs; two identities sharing a numeric ID get identical rights.

prompt: What is the difference between `su root` and `su - root`?
options: The hyphen runs root's startup scripts, simulating a full login
The hyphen skips the password prompt
Without the hyphen the command fails for normal users
The hyphen keeps you in your current directory
explanation: su - (or su -l) starts a login shell: it sources the target user's startup files and moves to their home directory. Plain su switches identity but keeps your existing environment.

prompt: After user1 runs `su - user100`, what do `whoami` and `logname` report?
options: whoami reports user100; logname reports user1
Both report user100
Both report user1
whoami reports user1; logname reports user100
explanation: whoami gives the effective (current) identity, while logname gives the real identity of whoever originally logged in — useful for spotting who is behind a switched session.

prompt: Whose password is required when root runs `su - user100`?
options: None — root switches to any account without a password prompt
user100's password
root's own password
Both root's and user100's
explanation: root may assume any identity unchallenged. A normal user must supply the target user's password to switch.

prompt: Which command should be used to edit /etc/sudoers, and why?
options: visudo — it validates the syntax before saving and prevents concurrent edits
vim — it is the standard editor for all configuration files
sudoedit — it is the only command permitted to open the file
nano — it will not corrupt the file's formatting
explanation: visudo edits a temporary copy (/etc/sudoers.tmp), checks the syntax, and refuses to save a broken file. A syntax error saved directly could lock everyone out of administrative access.

prompt: What does the sudoers entry `user10 ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` grant?
options: Full root authority for every command, without ever prompting for a password
Full root authority, prompting for user10's password each time
The ability to run only commands listed in NOPASSWD
Permission to change the root password without authenticating
explanation: NOPASSWD: suppresses the password prompt, and the trailing ALL means every command. Dropping NOPASSWD: makes sudo ask for the invoking user's own password.

prompt: Where should custom sudo rules preferably be placed, and what prefix denotes a group in them?
options: Drop-in files under /etc/sudoers.d, with % marking a group
Directly in /etc/sudoers, with @ marking a group
In /etc/security/sudo.conf, with & marking a group
In ~/.sudoers, with % marking a group
explanation: Drop-in files in /etc/sudoers.d keep the main file clean and survive package updates. A percentage sign identifies a group, e.g. %dba ALL=(ALL) ALL.

prompt: Under which account name does sudo record successful command execution in /var/log/secure?
options: The actual user who invoked sudo
root, since the command runs with root privileges
The owner of the command being run
No user name is recorded
explanation: This accountability is precisely why sudo is preferred over su: the log ties each privileged action to a real person, and privileges can be scoped to specific commands.

topic: Change File and Directory Owning User and Owning Group
prompt: Set both the owning user to user200 and the owning group to dba on the directory /tmp/dir10, applying it recursively.
explanation: chown accepts user:group to change both at once, and -R walks the tree. Changing ownership requires root privileges.

topic: Change File and Directory Owning User and Owning Group
prompt: Which statement about chown and chgrp is correct?
options: chown can set the owning user and group; chgrp sets only the group
chgrp can set the owning user and group; chown sets only the user
Both can set either attribute interchangeably
Neither requires root privileges
explanation: chown user:group handles both, whereas chgrp is limited to the owning group. Both need root privileges to reassign ownership.
